request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for specialized care due to circulatory failure. On admission, he presented with fever, myalgia, headache, and a rash. The patient did not report any ticks or eschar. The patient was initially treated for septic shock with intravenous normal saline. Spotted fever rickettsial infection was considered due to the presence of a rash, and the patient was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline. As the patient's condition worsened, he developed shortness of breath and hypoxemia, which indicated type 1 respiratory failure. An echocardiogram showed myocarditis and pulmonary edema leading to heart failure. Intravenous chloramphenicol was added to the treatment regimen, as it can be effective in cases like this. Three inotropes were required, including norepinephrine, dobutamine and dopamine, to maintain the patient's blood pressure. After increasing the steroids dosage, the patient began showing signs of improvement. The patient was extubated and transferred back to the High Dependency Unit of the medical ward. The patient was discharged from the hospital ten days following admission.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge Medications:
N/A

Follow-Up:
The patient was reviewed in the out-patient clinic, and he was asymptomatic. Further species identification was not possible due to unavailability of facilities. The patient did not turn up for the follow-up echocardiogram. 

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The clinical picture is a spotted fever group rickettsial infection with a rash, fever, myalgia and headache. It was complicated by myocarditis, pulmonary edema, shock and respiratory failure. The treatment was directed at rickettsial infection (doxycycline, chloramphenicol), and no species was identified.

Rickettsial infection is coded in ICD-10-AM under the spotted fever group, A77. Spotted fever, unspecified, is A77.9. The alternative of rickettsial myocarditis (I41.0*/A79) is a manifestation code and cannot be the principal diagnosis. The underlying etiology is the principal diagnosis, so the category is A77.

CODE: A77
